newsitem.title: FRANCE: Summary of labour unrest in France.
newsitem.headline: Summary of labour unrest in France.

text.p: The following is a summary of French labour unrest Prime Minister Alain Juppe has to contend with at a time of record unemployment and public spending restraint.
None so far has shown the momentum that produced crippling strikes in 1995. Main issues are rail reform, civil service pay and jobs, retirement, pensions, working hours and restructuring.
SNCF STATE RAILWAYS:

- February 5 strike called by Communist-led CGT. CFDT union, which organising protest rally but no strike, concedes it hard to sell campaign to public and members confused about issues. Limited disruption expected.
- January 30 strike call by CGT and CFDT, first and second largest rail unions, and small SUD-Rail union. Moderate success.
- Conflict is over reform to create state holding company to take over 134.2 billion francs of SNCF debts totalling 208 billion and become owner of rail infrastructure.
- Big SNCF unions say that under European deregulation pressures, this could threaten rail monopoly, public service and jobs. Minority unions accept reform to get out of debt problems.
- SUD Rail, strong in Paris, Lyon and other centres, called ineffective strike on January 21.
- Rail strike in Nov/Dec 1995 spearheaded public sector strike, but government no longer planning to curb SNCF early pension rights, which provoked cohesive union resistance.
CIVIL SERVICE/TEACHERS:
- March 6 strike call by all seven civil service unions over government pay offer on February 4 which does not allow "catch-up" for 1996 pay freeze.

- Government offering 2.8 percent total for 1997 and 1998, but nothing on 1996, for civil service staff including teachers as well as health service staff and local authority employees. One in five of employed are in public employment.
- Government also plans to cut some 6,000 jobs this year, including 2,700 among teachers.
- Crippling 1995 public sector strikes began with protest by civil servants over the 1996 pay freeze.

- Disputes over jobs and pay were source of October 17 strike, nationwide demonstrations and one-day strike in rail, air, school and postal services. Civil service ministry said one in three followed the call. Unions divided. Had been holding off on follow-up action after Juppe promised pay talks.
OTHER PUBLIC TRANSPORT:
- February 6 strike called by FO and CGT in regional bus and urban transit staff in follow-up to January 24 effective strike which was called by CGT, CFDT, Force Ouvriere, CFTC, FNCR.
- Unions are seeking retirement at 55, cut in working week without loss of pay, better conditions and job creation.
- Urban transport companies are mainly private ones with contracts with local authorities to provide public transport
- Paris RATP public transport services suffered little from sporadic union strike calls last year.
- Union calls, rejected by government, for use of "Robien law", which offers payroll charge relief in private sector when employers reduce work week to maintain employment levels.
BANKING SECTOR:
- January 28 Paris protest rally by 46 staff unions in 14 state and semi-state bank and financial sector groups. About 1,000 attended.
- Backdrop is gradual restructuring, government cuts and a banking climate which is still lacklustre. Most protests so far have been at company level and prospect of escalation limited.

- Employees of property lender Credit Foncier de France in sit-in at Paris headquarters since January 17. Held chairman hostage for first five days. Occupying bank to protest against government plan to wind it down.

- Unions fighting cutbacks at the Bank of France and seeking moratorium on job shedding in state and semi-state institutions. Credit Lyonnais staff worried about job cuts while government forced last year to call off sale of insurer GAN banking unit CIC, in part due to worries about job losses.
- Restructuring and privatisation plan being drawn up for GAN and unions also concerned over privatisation of Caisse Nationale de Prevoyance (CNP) insurance group.
- Banks are trying to negotiate deals individually on more flexible working time.
POWER UTILITIES:
- CGT says EU deregulation threat to jobs, public service.

- CGT, representing about half of staff at EdF electricity utility, opposes agreement which would allow a reduction of the working week to 32 hours with 35 hours pay and has vowed to "mobilise" members against it. FO opposed too.
- CFDT, CFTC and CGC unions signed deal on January 31.
- There have been sporadic, limited protests and stoppages in past but no power cuts.
PENSIONS:
- Bill introducing private pension funds has provoked union condemnation on grounds it will undermine the current benefit regime funded by welfare system, discourage pay rises.
- Bill condemned by major unions due to clause exempting employers paying into funds from Social Security levies on those contributions as well as tax relief for companies and employees.

- Unions hope to use second Senate reading of bill to secure change, arguing it will drain money from existing system and prompt employers to give pension fund contributions instead of pay rises, as the latter would be subject to full payroll charges.
- Unions -- the CGT, CFDT, CGC, CFTC and FSU -- refraining from predicting their response if clause not dropped.
- Bill due to go to Senate/National Assembly mixed committee for ironing out following second reading adoption in both houses of parliament.
RETIREMENT:
- Issue of early retirement reared its head after agreement by government in December to allow striking truck drivers take early retirement at 55 after minimum number of years' service.
- Local conflicts including protests by Bordeaux bus drivers and January 24 regional transport strike based on similar claims mixed with other conflicts over working time and conditions.

Government and opposition Socialists rule out generalised retirement at 55. Government says, if anything, strain on the pensions system will require people to work longer. National union leaders have dismissed, ducked or sidelined the issue.
DEFENCE:
- Government cutbacks and restructuring of sector have sparked sporadic protests or brief strikes by staff of state arms and defence companies and those working in naval dockyards.
AIRLINES:

- Restructuring at Air France and plans to merge it fully with its European unit Air France Europe sparked a series of one-day strikes last year, notably by pilots at Air France Europe worried about changed pay structures after the merger.
- December strike averted by setup of negotiating groups and Air France announced pay offer on January 30.
MAIN NATIONAL UNION CONFEDERATIONS
CFDT - Socialist. Leader Nicole Notat
CGT - Communist. hardline. Leader Louis Viannet
Force Ouvriere. hardline. Leader March Blondel
CFTC - Christian. moderate. Leader Alain Deleu
CGC - White-collar, moderate. Leader Marc Vilbenoit
FSU - Teachers/civil servants. Leader Michel Deschamps
